source.version: Undated working paper titled 'Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation'. The document prints no date, venue, version label, or page numbers. PDF metadata give creation date 2024-09-07 (Microsoft Word for Microsoft 365), and the reference list includes items dated 2024. The PDF saved for c162 is byte-for-byte identical to this PDF. The current c007 search record instead names 'Artificial intelligence and its impact on creativity and diversity: An empirical study of large language model-generated product ideas' (Production and Operations Management, 2026; DOI 10.1177/10591478261474243; arXiv 2607.27553), and lists 'Ideas Are Dimes a Dozen' as an earlier title. Those version links and the later version's study coverage are unverified leads, not facts established by this saved PDF. This form's eligibility decision applies to the saved working paper.
source.title_on_document: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation

supplement.where: Appendix A (Quantile Regression Results) and Appendix B (Supplementary Regression Tables), pp. 30-36 of this PDF. Both appendices are also present in the current markdown conversion (lines 506-763). The document names no separate online supplement.
supplement.holds: Table A.1 (p. 30) gives the quantile-regression coefficients and confidence intervals behind Figure 4; Table A.1 does not state the confidence level. Appendix B (pp. 30-36) gives the full mixed-model tables for purchase intent and novelty, including random-effect variances, ICC where reported, R2, and analysis counts: 200 respondents and 7,982 ratings for purchase intent (p. 31), 201 respondents and 8,023 ratings for novelty (p. 34), and 400 ideas in each model. It also gives the alternative-weight, idea-level simple, zero-shot-baseline, and ordered-logistic models. No standard errors are printed.

paper_design_summary: The paper compares three pools of new-product ideas for US college students priced at $50 or less: 200 ideas randomly sampled from those written by students in a 2021 product design course before LLMs were widely available, 100 ideas generated by GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314) with zero-shot prompting, and 100 generated by GPT-4 with six example student ideas (few-shot). No study participant received AI assistance. College-age US raters on Prolific scored each idea's purchase intent and novelty, and the authors computed pairwise cosine similarity of Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings within each pool.

studies.label: Student vs GPT-4 product-idea pools (the paper's Studies 1, 2, and 3 analyze the same 400 ideas: 200 student, 100 GPT-4 zero-shot, 100 GPT-4 few-shot)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was assigned to AI. The comparison is defined by idea source (students in 2021, GPT-4 zero-shot, GPT-4 few-shot). Randomization appears only in sampling the 200 student ideas from the course pool (p. 10) and in showing ideas to raters in random order, randomized at the idea level (p. 12).
assignment.quote: For our experiment, we utilize three different pools of ideas, namely student-generated ideas, GPT-4-generated ideas with zero-shot prompting and GPT-4-generated ideas with few-shot prompting.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 4 (three pools, student ideas from 2021, random selection of 200); p. 12, Section 5 (ideas shown to raters in random order)

arms.name: Student ideas
arms.description: 200 ideas randomly selected from those written by students in a 2021 product design and innovation course at an unnamed elite university, before LLMs were widely available. Each idea is a title plus a paragraph, average 63 words. Produced without AI.

arms.name: GPT-4 zero-shot
arms.description: 100 ideas generated by gpt-4-0314 (temperature 0.7) from the prompt given to the students, ten per request, 40-80 words requested. To stay within the context window, earlier ideas were compressed into summaries and fed back with a request for different ideas. Average 69 words. No person took part in production beyond the authors' prompts.

arms.name: GPT-4 few-shot
arms.description: 100 ideas generated by gpt-4-0314 with the same prompt plus six highly rated ideas from a separate student set that completed the same exercise. Average 71 words. Average cosine similarity between the six examples and the 100 ideas is 0.33, maximum 0.51 (p. 12).

participants.exclusions: None stated. The compared units are ideas (200 student, 100 zero-shot, 100 few-shot). The paper does not say how many of the course's 50 students wrote the 200 sampled ideas.
participants.who: Idea producers: students in a 2021 product design and innovation course at an unnamed elite university. 50 students took part in the course's innovation challenge. GPT-4 produced the other 200 ideas from the authors' prompts. Raters (not idea producers, in no arm): college-age individuals from the United States recruited on Prolific. Appendix B reports 200 respondents analyzed for purchase intent (7,982 ratings, p. 31) and 201 analyzed for novelty (8,023 ratings, p. 34). Rater overlap between these analyses is not stated. Each respondent rated about 40 ideas, and each idea was rated about 20 times (p. 12).
participants.country: Not stated for the students (the university is not named). Raters from the United States (p. 12).
participants.quote: In this course, 50 students participated in an innovation challenge to come up with ideas for a physical product marketed to college students for $50 or less
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 4 (students); p. 12, Section 5 (raters); Appendix B pp. 31 and 34 (N RespondentID 200 and 201)

ai_tool.how_used: The authors prompted GPT-4 directly: a system prompt casting it as a creative entrepreneur, user prompts asking for ten ideas of 40-80 words each, compressed summaries of earlier ideas fed back to avoid repeats, and, for few-shot, six example ideas. No participant used AI. The AI output is compared with pre-LLM human output.

task.description: Generate ideas for a physical product (not a service or software) targeted at college students in the United States that could sell for $50 or less (GPT-4 prompt: less than about USD 50). Each idea is a title plus a paragraph (GPT-4 was asked for 40-80 words).
task.duration: Not stated for the student challenge (part of a one-semester course) or for the GPT-4 runs. The Summary says, as a general statement, that two hundred ideas can be generated by one human interacting with GPT-4 in about 15 minutes (p. 26).

outcomes.name: Purchase intent (idea quality), Study 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Prolific respondents (college-age, United States) gave five-box purchase intent for each idea, weighted 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 (Jamieson and Bass 1989, spelled 'Jameson' in the text) into a purchase probability used as idea quality. Main analysis: linear mixed-effects model with two source fixed effects (humans baseline) and random intercepts and slopes for respondents and ideas. The paper calls it 'our primary purchase-intent analysis' (pp. 23-24). Appendix B: intercept 0.40, 200 respondents, 400 ideas, 7,982 observations (pp. 30-31). Robustness (Section 8.2.1, pp. 23-24; Appendix B pp. 31-33): Ulrich and Eppinger weights (0.4 definitely, 0.2 probably, 0 otherwise) give zero-shot 0.02 (CI 0.01 – 0.03, p = 0.001) and few-shot 0.03 (CI 0.02 – 0.04, p < 0.001); idea-level simple regression on 400 ideas (Appendix B intercept 1.62, so not the 0-1 scale, and the paper does not name the scale); cumulative link mixed model; ordered logistic regression; unweighted model with zero-shot baseline (Source [Student] -0.24, CI -0.35 – -0.12, p < 0.001). Figure 1 (p. 13) prints Mean/Std labels (0.41/0.117, 0.366/0.101, 0.361/0.111) that equal the novelty labels of Figure 3 and conflict with the text means. The text says only that the standard deviations are comparable, so no purchase-intent SDs are usable.

contrasts.reported: Mean purchase intent: GPT-4 zero-shot 46.4% vs humans 40.4% (p. 13). Mixed model: β = 0.059; 95% CI [0.031, 0.088]; t(246) = 4.06, p < 0.001 (p. 14). Appendix B: Source [Zero-Shot] 0.06, CI 0.03 – 0.09, p < 0.001 (p. 30). Simple regression: 0.256 points (95% CI [0.15, 0.37]; t = 4.602, p < 0.001) (p. 24), Appendix B 0.26, CI 0.15 – 0.37, p < 0.001 (p. 32). CLMM: β = 0.395; 95% CI [0.215, 0.575]; z = 4.31, p < 0.001 (p. 24). Ordered logistic regression: odds ratio 1.48, CI 1.24 – 1.78, p < 0.001 (p. 33).
contrasts.locator: p. 13 (text below Figure 1); p. 14, Section 5; p. 24, Section 8.2.1; Appendix B pp. 30, 32, 33

contrasts.reported: Mean purchase intent: GPT-4 few-shot 49.3% vs humans 40.4% (p. 13). Mixed model: β = 0.089; 95% CI [0.060, 0.12]; t(223) = 5.93, p < 0.001 (p. 14). Appendix B: Source [Few-Shot] 0.09, CI 0.06 – 0.12, p < 0.001 (p. 30). Simple regression: 0.358 points (95% CI [0.25, 0.47]; t = 6.435, p < 0.001) (p. 24), Appendix B 0.36, CI 0.25 – 0.47, p < 0.001 (p. 32). CLMM: β = 0.581; 95% CI [0.400, 0.762]; z = 6.30, p < 0.001 (p. 24). Ordered logistic regression: odds ratio 1.79, CI 1.49 – 2.14, p < 0.001 (p. 33).
contrasts.locator: p. 13 (text below Figure 1); p. 14, Section 5; p. 24, Section 8.2.1; Appendix B pp. 30, 32, 33

contrasts.reported: Two AI prompting pools, no human producers: β = 0.03; 95% CI [-0.01, 0.06]; t(199) = 1.892, p = 0.06, described as 'weakly significantly different' (p. 14). Appendix B unweighted model with zero-shot baseline: Source [Few-Shot] 0.12, CI -0.00 – 0.24, p = 0.058 (p. 32). The point estimate favors few-shot (means 49.3% vs 46.4%, p. 13).

outcomes.name: Average pairwise cosine similarity within each idea pool, Study 2 (Section 6.1)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of Google Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) embeddings for each pair of ideas within a pool, averaged over all pairs (Table 1). Higher similarity means less diverse, so the sign is reversed and direction is coded on diversity. Robustness (Section 8.2.2, p. 24): mean edge length of a minimum spanning tree over the 512-dimensional embeddings, from 0 (not diverse) to 1 (very diverse): students 0.53, GPT-4 zero-shot 0.33, GPT-4 few-shot 0.3, with no test.

contrasts.reported: Average cosine similarity of all ideas: GPT-4 zero-shot 0.415 (100 ideas) vs students 0.221 (200 ideas) (Table 1). No pairwise test is printed for this contrast. Three-group one-way ANOVA: η² = 0.455, 95% CI [-0.210, -0.204], F(2, 29598) = 12340.95, p < 0.001 (p. 15); Figure 2 prints F(2, 29598) = 12340.951, p<0.001 (p. 16). MST mean edge distance: zero-shot 0.33 vs students 0.53 (p. 24).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text; p. 16, Figure 2; p. 24, Section 8.2.2

contrasts.reported: Average cosine similarity of all ideas: GPT-4 few-shot 0.428 (100 ideas) vs students 0.221 (200 ideas) (Table 1). No pairwise test is printed for this contrast. Same three-group ANOVA: η² = 0.455, 95% CI [-0.210, -0.204], F(2, 29598) = 12340.95, p < 0.001 (p. 15). MST mean edge distance: few-shot 0.3 vs students 0.53 (p. 24).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text; p. 16, Figure 2; p. 24, Section 8.2.2

contrasts.reported: Two groups: human ideas have a significantly smaller cosine similarity than GPT-4-generated ideas (η² = 0.358, 95% CI [-0.197, -0.190], F(1, 24649) = 13715.82, p < 0.001) (p. 15). No pooled GPT-4 similarity level is printed.

Zero-shot GPT-4 ideas exhibit a significantly smaller cosine similarity than few-shot GPT-4 ideas (η² = 0.004, 95% CI [-0.018, -0.010], F(1, 9898) = 44.24, p < 0.001) (p. 15). Levels 0.415 (zero-shot) vs 0.428 (few-shot) (Table 1). MST mean edge distance: few-shot 0.3 vs zero-shot 0.33 (p. 24).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text; p. 24, Section 8.2.2

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity within pool (higher means less diverse); minimum-spanning-tree mean edge distance as robustness
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each pool (200 student, 100 zero-shot, 100 few-shot). The student pool mixes ideas from different students; each GPT-4 pool comes from one model.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way ANOVA over pairwise similarities (F tests with pair-level degrees of freedom). The 95% CIs printed beside η² are negative, so they are not intervals for η², and the paper does not say what they bound. The paper describes no adjustment for the dependence among pairs that share an idea. No test for the MST measure.
diversity_detail.notes: No study participant received AI assistance: this compares a pool of AI ideas with a pool of human ideas. Pair counts are not printed. The ANOVA degrees of freedom are retained exactly as printed on p. 15; the paper does not explain the pair construction or exclusions underlying those denominators.

outcomes.name: Fraction of overlapping ideas (cosine similarity > 0.8), Study 2 (Section 6.1)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: An idea counts as overlapping when its USE cosine similarity with a previously added idea exceeds θ = 0.8 (text, pp. 8 and 14). The Table 1 notes instead define the fraction by an idea's average pairwise similarity to all other ideas in the pool exceeding 0.8 (p. 15). The paper presents overlap as its first measure of flexibility (pp. 7-8). Robustness thresholds (p. 24): 0.7 gives 25 (zero-shot) and 37 (few-shot) overlapping ideas, 0.75 gives 16 and 23, and 0.85 gives 2 and 1. Direction is coded on diversity: more overlap means less diverse.

contrasts.reported: Fraction of ideas in pool with cosine similarity >0.8: students 0, GPT-4 zero-shot 0.05 (Table 1). Binomial test: human fraction 95% CI [0.0, 0.0184]; RD = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.093, -0.007], p < 0.001 (p. 15).
Fraction of ideas in pool with cosine similarity >0.8: students 0, GPT-4 few-shot 0.07 (Table 1). Binomial test: RD = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.120, -0.020], p < 0.001 (p. 15).
The difference between the two GPT-4 pools is not significant: RD = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.086, 0.046], p = 0.56 (p. 15). Fractions 0.05 (zero-shot) and 0.07 (few-shot) (Table 1).

diversity_detail.metric: Share of ideas in a pool whose USE cosine similarity exceeds 0.8 (overlap)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the ideas previously added to its pool (text, pp. 8 and 14). The Table 1 notes say each idea's average pairwise similarity to all other ideas in the pool (p. 15).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Binomial test on the fraction of overlapping ideas: risk differences with 95% CIs and p-values.
diversity_detail.notes: The definition differs between the text and the Table 1 notes. The paper calls this flexibility. It is coded diversity because the student pool mixes different people's ideas, while each GPT-4 pool comes from one model.

outcomes.name: Estimated number of discoverable ideas (capture-recapture), Study 2 (Section 6.2)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Capture-recapture model of Kornish and Ulrich (2011): p(n) = e^(-an), u(n) = (1/a)(1 - e^(-an)), T = 1/a, with overlap defined at the 0.8 cosine threshold. T estimates the number of unique ideas the process can generate. The paper presents it as its second measure of flexibility (p. 8). It also says that prompting with examples 'seems to further reduce the estimated number of unique ideas available to the process' (p. 17), with no test. Direction is coded on diversity.

contrasts.reported: 5 of the 100 zero-shot ideas were essentially similar to an idea already generated; u(100) is 0.95; estimate of T of 966 ideas (p. 17). Human-generated ideas were all unique (p. 17), so the number of unique ideas would be 'infinitely large' (p. 15).

7 of the 100 few-shot ideas were redundant; u(100) is 0.93; estimate of T of 680 ideas (p. 17). Human-generated ideas were all unique (p. 17), so the number of unique ideas would be 'infinitely large' (p. 15).

diversity_detail.metric: Estimated size of the opportunity space T from the rate of overlapping ideas
diversity_detail.computed_over: The sequence of ideas within each pool, each idea against earlier ideas
diversity_detail.notes: No interval or test is reported for T. T is computed from the same overlap counts as S1-O3.

outcomes.name: Perceived novelty, Study 2 (Section 6.3)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Prolific respondents answered 'Relative to other products you have seen, how novel do you consider the idea for this new product?' on 0 / 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 / 1 (not at all to extremely novel), based on Shibayama et al. (2021). Linear mixed-effects model with two source fixed effects (humans baseline) and random intercepts and slopes for respondents and ideas. Appendix B: intercept 0.41, 201 respondents, 400 ideas, 8,023 observations (pp. 33-34). Robustness (Section 8.2.2, pp. 24-25; Appendix B pp. 34-36): idea-level simple regression on 400 ideas (Appendix B intercept 1.64, so not the 0-1 scale, and the paper does not name the scale); CLMM; ordered logistic regression; zero-shot-baseline models (Source [Student] 0.04, CI 0.01 – 0.07, p = 0.008, p. 35; unweighted 0.15, CI 0.05 – 0.26, p = 0.004, p. 34). The Figure 3 note says 'Novelty based on mTurk assessment' (p. 18), while the text says the raters were on Prolific (pp. 12, 17). Average novelty of each source's top-decile ideas: students 0.45, zero-shot 0.35, few-shot 0.33 (Table 3, p. 20).

outcomes.name: Quality of the best ideas: share of the pooled top decile by purchase intent, Study 3 (Section 7)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: All 400 ideas ranked by mean purchase intent. The top 40 (top 10%) are listed in Table 2 (pp. 19-20). Table 3 gives each source's share of the top decile and the average quality and novelty of its top-decile ideas, and a chi-square test compares the shares with equal representation (20, 10, 10). Robustness: top 5% and top 15% (Table 4, p. 25). Table 2 lists 42 rows (20 few-shot, 17 zero-shot, 5 student, with the last rows tied at 0.61), while the text and Table 3 count 40 ideas with 15 from zero-shot. Table 4's top-5% source fractions are printed as 1/20, 6/20, and 14/20; these do not sum to a complete partition of the stated top 5%. The printed values are retained without attempting to correct the paper.

contrasts.treatment_arm: GPT-4 zero-shot and GPT-4 few-shot (15/40 and 20/40)
contrasts.reported: Fraction of the top decile of pooled ideas from this source: students 5/40, GPT-4 zero-shot 15/40, GPT-4 few-shot 20/40; average quality of top decile 0.62, 0.64, 0.66; average novelty of top decile 0.45, 0.35, 0.33 (Table 3, p. 20). Among the top 40 ideas, 35 (87.5%) were generated by GPT-4, 7 GPT-4 ideas for every human idea. Chi-square test of equal representation (20, 10 and 10): x² = 26.39, p < 0.001, df = 2 (p. 20). Top 5%: 1/20, 6/20, 14/20 (average quality 0.64, 0.67, 0.68). Top 15%: 11/60, 22/60, 27/60 (average quality 0.60, 0.62, 0.64) (Table 4, p. 25).
contrasts.locator: pp. 19-20, Table 2; p. 20, Table 3 and text; p. 25, Table 4

outcomes.name: Quantile regression of idea-level mean rating on AI source, Study 3 (Section 7)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: MeanRating ~ SourceAI at quantiles 0.1 to 0.9 (step 0.1), where SourceAI = 1 for GPT-4 (zero-shot and few-shot pooled) and 0 for student ideas (Appendix A, p. 30). The dependent variable is 'the average idea quality ratings' (p. 21). Intercepts run from 1 to 2.181822, so the rating scale is not the 0-1 purchase probability, and the paper does not say which scale it is. The number of observations is not printed.

company_involvement.description: Authors list university affiliations only (The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania; Cornell Tech and Johnson College of Business, Cornell University). Funding came from the Mack Institute for Innovation Management at the Wharton School. OpenAI's GPT-4 is the model studied, and the document states no company role in the research.

eligibility.reason: For the saved working paper, criterion 1 is not met: students produced ideas before widespread LLM availability, and the authors directly prompted GPT-4 to generate the comparison pools (pp. 10-12, Section 4). Random selection of student ideas and random presentation to raters are not random assignment of people to AI assistance (pp. 10 and 12). Criterion 2 is unclear independently of criterion 1: the source course had 50 students, but the paper does not state how many distinct students contributed the 200 sampled ideas analyzed (p. 10). People counts therefore remain null. The 200 and 201 analyzed raters (Appendix B, pp. 31 and 34) evaluate outputs and do not count as creative-task participants. Criterion 3 is met: novelty is rated on product ideas and similarity is computed from idea embeddings (pp. 14-18); purchase intent also evaluates the ideas (pp. 12-14). The saved document is AI-versus-human context evidence and remains outside the core regardless of the unresolved student count. This decision must not be transferred to the later journal version named in candidates.json without reviewing that version and any added experiments or reanalyses.

one_line_finding: In this AI-versus-human comparison (no study participant received AI assistance), GPT-4 product ideas had higher mean purchase intent than 2021 student ideas (zero-shot 46.4 percent and few-shot 49.3 percent vs 40.4 percent; p. 13), lower rated novelty (36.7 and 36.1 vs 40.6 percent; p. 17), higher average pairwise cosine similarity (0.415 and 0.428 vs 0.221; Table 1, p. 15), and 35 of the 40 top-ranked ideas (Table 3, p. 20).
open_questions: Figure 1 (p. 13, 'Purchase Intent by Idea Type') prints Mean 0.41 / 0.366 / 0.361 and Std 0.117 / 0.101 / 0.111, the same labels as the novelty Figure 3 (p. 18), while the text gives purchase-intent means of 40.4, 46.4, and 49.3 percent (p. 13). No purchase-intent SDs are printed elsewhere.

Table 2 (pp. 19-20, 'Top 10% Ideas by Purchase Intent') lists 42 ideas (20 few-shot, 17 zero-shot, 5 student, with the last rows tied at 0.61), while the text and Table 3 count 40 ideas with 15 from zero-shot (p. 20).
The Table 1 notes (p. 15) define the overlap fraction by an idea's average pairwise similarity, while the text (pp. 8 and 14) defines overlap against any previously added idea.

The number of distinct students whose output was analyzed is not stated. Section 4 reports 50 students in the source course but samples 200 ideas from 'these challenges' (p. 10). This leaves criterion 2 unclear; it does not change the saved paper's exclusion under criterion 1.
The Figure 3 note says 'Novelty based on mTurk assessment' (p. 18), while the text says the novelty raters were on Prolific (pp. 12 and 17).

The scales of the idea-level simple regressions (intercepts 1.62 and 1.64, pp. 32 and 34) and of the quantile regression (intercepts 1 to 2.181822, p. 30) are not named. They are not the 0-1 purchase-probability scale.
The ANOVA degrees of freedom (F(2, 29598), F(1, 24649), F(1, 9898), p. 15) are printed without analysis pair counts or an explanation of pair construction, exclusions, or dependence adjustments.

Resolved for screening: the introduction reports AI-versus-human summary means (purchase intent 0.48 vs 0.40; novelty 0.36 vs 0.41; p. 3), while Sections 5 and 6.3 report the individual GPT-4 pools (pp. 13 and 17). These are differently aggregated descriptive summaries, not an eligibility uncertainty. The extraction retains the printed per-pool values and derives no pooled estimate.

Resolved record linkage for the saved documents: the c007 and c162 PDFs are byte-for-byte identical and have the same title, authors, and analyses. They must not be counted as independent samples. No other record was edited or merged during this finalization.

Shared-sample lead checked at source: c014, 'Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance', p. 5, describes 100 randomly chosen Wharton MBA student ideas and states: 'This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.' This saved c007 PDF describes 200 sampled ideas from a 2021 course (p. 10). Exact idea and participant overlap remains unconfirmed.

Version coverage remains unverified: the current c007 search record names the later journal title 'Artificial intelligence and its impact on creativity and diversity: An empirical study of large language model-generated product ideas' (DOI 10.1177/10591478261474243; arXiv 2607.27553), rather than the title on the saved PDF. Review that version to establish its relation to this working paper and whether it adds any eligible human experiments or reanalyses; any reanalysis must inherit the original experiment's design class.

Table 4 (p. 25) prints top-5% source fractions 1/20, 6/20, and 14/20, which do not sum to a complete partition. The printed values are retained; the intended counts and treatment of ties need clarification.
notes: Reconciled from forms A and B against the markdown and every PDF page (1-36). The paper's Studies 1, 2, and 3 analyze one set of 400 ideas, so the form records one study. Appendix B reports 200 raters analyzed for purchase intent and 201 for novelty (pp. 31 and 34); their overlap is not stated. Arm counts are ideas (200, 100, 100), so people counts are null. ai_available_when_produced is mixed because the student pool was written without AI and the GPT-4 pools were produced by the model itself. Few-shot vs zero-shot contrasts are coded other because both arms are model output. Directions for diversity outcomes are coded on diversity: higher similarity or more overlap means lower diversity. Outcome map: final S1-O1 = A O1 = B O1; S1-O2 = A O3 = B O3; S1-O3 = A O4 = B O4 (overlap part); S1-O4 = A O5 = B O4 (T part); S1-O5 = A O6 = B O2; S1-O6 = A O2 (top-decile part) = B O5; S1-O7 = A O2 (quantile part) = B O6. Not listed as outcomes: the novelty-purchase intent correlation (-0.08, 95% CI [-0.176, 0.016], p=0.12; p. 18), the descriptive Table 2, and the check that few-shot ideas did not copy the six examples (average similarity 0.33, maximum 0.51; p. 12). IRB: University of Pennsylvania, May 2023, Protocol #853634 (p. 12). Ratings were collected in May and June 2023 (p. 23). Locators use one-based PDF page numbers. The document prints none. Final review read the entire current markdown, including Appendices A and B, checked the reported statistics against the PDF, and inspected the embedded figures. No c007 challenge files were present; final challenge counts therefore remain zero. All reconciliation differences were already marked resolved, and the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical provenance. open_items.item: Figure 1 purchase-intent means/SDs conflict with its text and duplicate Figure 3 labels (pp. 13 and 18). Author correction or original rating summaries would settle the intended statistics; output scoring itself is established.

Table 2 displays more ideas than the top-decile count in the text and Table 3 (pp. 19-20). Authors must clarify the intended counts and treatment of ties. This affects result extraction, not eligibility.

Overlap is defined against any earlier idea in the text but against average similarity in Table 1's note (pp. 8, 14-15). Analysis code and the idea-similarity data would identify the implemented rule; both definitions score outputs.

Distinct students represented among the analyzed ideas are unknown (p. 10). Authors must confirm the analyzed ideator count, or supply the idea-to-student mapping. This affects criterion 2 only; criterion 1 still excludes the saved paper.

Novelty rater platform: Prolific in the text versus mTurk in Figure 3's note (pp. 12, 17-18). Authors can confirm the platform; either platform supplies human ratings of output and does not alter eligibility.
The response scales for the simple and quantile regressions are not named (pp. 30, 32, 34). Authors must confirm the coding; these remain output-scored outcomes regardless of scale.

Pair counts, pair construction, exclusions, and dependence treatment underlying the ANOVA degrees of freedom are unspecified (p. 15). Analysis data and code would settle the inferential unit and precision, not the people-count or output-scoring criteria.
Introduction summary means versus per-pool means (pp. 3, 13, 17): no further information is needed for screening. Retain the printed per-pool statistics without deriving a pooled estimate.
c162 duplicate is settled: the two saved PDFs are byte-for-byte identical, so the sample is shared. This linkage changes neither design nor eligibility; no additional source is needed.

Exact student/idea overlap with c014 remains unknown despite its explicit reference to Girotra et al. (2023) (c014 p. 5; c007 p. 10). Authors can supply a common idea/participant mapping. This concerns deduplication, not the saved study's eligibility.

Later journal-version coverage is unverified. Read the journal version to establish identity and inspect any added human experiments or reanalyses against all three criteria. The final no decision here is limited to the saved working paper.
Table 4's top-5% fractions do not form a complete partition (p. 25). Authors must clarify the intended counts and ties; this does not affect eligibility.
